newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany braces for 10th anniversary of Hess death.
newsitem.headline: Germany braces for 10th anniversary of Hess death.

text.p: Several hundred Germans staged weekend demonstrations against right-wing extremists, expected to hold neo-Nazi rallies next week on the 10th anniversary of the death of Hitler's deputy Rudolf Hess.
Police in the east German town of Quedlinburg said about 500 people held a demonstration on Saturday evening against the annual neo-Nazi rallies marking Hess's death, aged 93, on August 17, 1987.

Each year, hundreds of neo-Nazis try to outfox police by holding a memorial rally for Hess on the anniversary of his death. The gatherings are outlawed, but the extremists have succeeded in staging large demonstrations.
The date has become a rallying point for the radical right in Germany and several other European countries in recent years.
Last year police detained around 160 right-wing activists at one banned march in the western town of Worms. In Sweden, Norway and Denmark, hundreds of neo-Nazis clashed with police last year.
Authorities in Quedlinburg said no disturbances were reported at the demonstration on Saturday night.

But in the western town of Luebeck, a hotbed of recent right-wing extremism, the local Luebeck Alliance Against Racism said that a group of 20 neo-Nazis was passing out leaflets claiming that Hess was murdered by the Allies 10 years ago in Berlin's Spandau prison.

Hess, who hanged himself with an electric cord, parachuted into Scotland in 1941 to press for an Anglo-German alliance against the Soviet Union. He spent the rest of his life in custody, the last two decades as the sole inmate of Spandau.
"We are completely baffled that the police in Luebeck were were not better prepared to stop this action by the neo-Nazis," said Christoph Kleine, spokesman for the Luebeck group.
He said Luebeck was a preferred target for "neo-Nazi provocations", citing a series of firebombings of churches.
